question: Using the customary setting of the mathematics used for quantum mechanics, is it possible to prove the existence of Gödelßs god-like entities?

7.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: No. The mathematics that is customary in quantum theory is the standard functional-analytic apparatus on a complex separable Hilbert space, essentially ZFC set theory plus normed linear algebra, spectral theory and measure theory. That apparatus provides a language of states, observables as self-adjoint operators, and probabilities via the Born rule, but it contains no primitive modal operator and no structure of accessible possible worlds.

Gödel’s ontological argument is formulated in a quantified modal logic of the S5 type, with the necessity operator interpreted as holding in every metaphysically possible world and with the axiom that a positive property is positive in every world. A proof of the existence of a God-like being in that sense requires a Kripke-style semantics for the modal part, or at the very least an explicit model of possible worlds in which the usual axioms of positivity, necessary existence from maximal positivity, etc., are validated.

The Hilbert-space formalism of ordinary quantum mechanics does not supply such a semantics, and it is not a part of the customary physical mathematics to adjoin one. One can formalise the first-order part of Gödel’s axioms in ZF(C), but the modal interpretation needed for the essential step “if a property is positive then it is necessarily positive” and for the necessity of existence is external to the analytic setting routinely used in quantum physics. Hence within the customary mathematical setting of quantum mechanics there is no internal proof of the existence of Gödel’s god-like entities without first extending the framework beyond standard functional analysis.

1.text:
In the physics literature quantum mechanics is done in ordinary classical mathematics. 
A theory is formulated as a complex separable Hilbert space H, a * algebra of
observables, self-adjoint operators, spectral measures, states as normalised
positive linear functionals etc. All of that is defined in ZFC, first order
logic, and in practice the usual classical meta-theory. Quantum logic is a
derivative orthomodular lattice structure on the projection lattice of H; it
is still interpreted in the classical meta-theory.

Godel's ontological argument is a formal argument in first order modal
logic S5. With the standard Godel definitions

* P is positive
* P is essentially positive if necessarily positive in all worlds in which
E exists
* G is God-like iff E essentially has all positive properties

and the axioms

A1  □P → P,
A2  P → □P,
A3  P & Q → R etc. for the closure of positivity,

Godel shows in S5

    □◇∃x G(x) → ∃x G(x)

and from the axiom that God-likeness is positive, ◇∃x G(x), he gets
∃x G(x) and indeed □∃x G(x). The argument is valid in S5; it is formalizable
in any meta-theory strong enough to formalize first order modal logic with a
finite set of axioms, in particular in the ZFC + classical logic in which
Hilbert spaces, C*-algebras and all the usual quantum mechanical formalism is
defined.

What it does not give is a mathematical theorem about Hilbert spaces or about
numbers. The only non-logical content is the definition of “positive
property’’ and the metaphysical closure principles A1–A3 together with the
claim ◇∃x G(x). Those principles are not theorems of arithmetic, of set
theory or of the mathematical formalism of quantum mechanics. They are
philosophical premises about value and modality. Conditional on them the
conclusion is a theorem of S5 and hence a theorem of the meta-theory in which
quantum mechanics is written down. Unconditionally there is no mathematical
proof of the existence of a Godelian God-like being from the equations of
quantum mechanics.

In the usual sense in which a mathematical proof is a derivation from
uncontroversial mathematical axioms the existence of Godel’s God-like
entities is not proved, and it cannot be proved by changing the formal
machinery from Boolean to the orthomodular lattice of projections, because the
latter is always interpreted in a classical meta-theory. That is the
well-known fact that the customary mathematics of quantum mechanics is the
ordinary mathematics to which Godel’s incompleteness theorems apply: a
consistent, recursively axiomatizable, sufficiently strong system cannot
prove its own consistency, let alone an unformalized metaphysical
existence claim. The physics adds no new logical strength.

5.text:
In the physics literature the “mathematics of quantum mechanics’’ is the
mathematics of complex Hilbert spaces, bounded operators, spectral theory
and C*-algebras, i.e. ordinary analysis on top of the set-theoretic
foundation ZF+AC in which the Hilbert space is constructed. 
That foundation is more than enough, in a purely formal sense, to write
down first order modal logic S5 and the primitive notion of a property
with Gödel’s axioms

* P is positive → ¬P is not positive
* If P is positive and P→Q is provable then Q is positive
* Necessary existence is positive
* etc.

and to carry through Gödel’s deduction

God-like := essence of all positive properties
Positive → possibly instantiated
Necessarily, if God-like is instantiated then it is necessarily
instantiated

in the meta-theory ZFC. In that purely syntactic sense the ontological
argument is a theorem of the background set theory that underlies the
Hilbert-space formalism, and it is conditional on the metaphysical axiom
schema that defines what is to count as a ‘positive property’ and that
necessary existence is positive.

In the customary physical formalism itself the notions that drive the
argument have no definition. The language of quantum mechanics is the
language of vectors, self-adjoint operators, spectra, states,
expectation values, etc. It contains no predicate ‘P is positive in the
Gödel sense’, no primitive modal operator □ for metaphysical
necessity, and no way to make the notion of an ‘essence of all positive
properties’ a vector, an operator or any other object of the
Hilbert-space theory. The axioms of positivity are not empirically
grounded, they are not part of spectral theory or C*–algebra theory,
and they are not provable from the physical postulates of quantum
mechanics.

Hence the customary QM mathematics can at best host the logical
deduction as an exercise in the background set theory. It gives only a
conditional logical consistency result: if you accept Gödel’s
metaphysical axioms for positivity and necessity, then in the model of
S5 there is an entity possessing all positive properties. That is a
formal existence in the model of the modal theory, not an existence
statement inside the physical Hilbert-space formalism and not a
physically testable consequence of quantum mechanics. In the
substantive physical sense the existence of Gödel’s god-like entities
cannot be proved, and indeed cannot even be stated, in the ordinary
mathematics used for quantum mechanics.

3.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: No. The mathematics that is actually used in ordinary quantum mechanics is just ordinary classical mathematics. In the usual presentation it is ZF set theory together with the theory of separable complex Hilbert spaces, self-adjoint operators, spectral measures, etc. That is a fragment of ZFC.

Gödel’s ontological argument is a modal-logical argument. It is a derivation in S5 modal logic from a set of metaphysical axioms about the notion of a “positive’’ property, e.g.

P1.  □∀P[Pos(P) → Pos(□P)], 
P2.  ∀P[Pos(P) → ¬Pos(¬P)], 
P3.  Pos(P) → Pos(∃x P(x)), etc.,

together with the definition God ≡ ∀P[Pos(P) → P(x)]. From those premises S5 gives
∃x God(x) and indeed □∃x God(x).

The argument is not a theorem of ZF, let alone of functional analysis. The positivity axioms are not mathematical axioms; they are substantive, essentially theological, claims about essence and modality. Once the S5 system is coded up in the set-theoretic meta-theory in which Hilbert spaces live you can of course formalise the derivation, and relative to the positivity axioms the conclusion is a theorem of the formalised S5. That is the sense in which Gödel was able to write the argument down at all.

It is not a theorem of the mathematics of quantum mechanics, and a fortiori it is not a theorem that follows from physics. The existence of a Gödelian god-like entity is independent of ZFC, and in any case the quantum-logical propositional calculus that is sometimes associated with quantum mechanics is orthomodular, not Boolean and not S5. No unconditional proof of ∃x God(x) from Hilbert space theory, operator algebras or any other ordinary quantum-mechanical formalism is known, and on standard views none is expected, because the premises of the ontological proof are not mathematical.

4.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: No. The mathematics that is actually customary in quantum mechanics is the standard classical mathematics of separable complex Hilbert spaces, bounded/ self-adjoint operators, spectral theory and functional analysis, i.e. essentially ZFC plus the usual classical first-order logic of analysis. 

Gödel’s ontological argument is a modal argument. Its formalisation requires the S5 modal language with the axiom that a positive property is necessarily positive, and the usual closure conditions on the accessibility relation for S5. In the Hilbert-space formalism there is no primitive modal operator, no Kripke frame, and no natural interpretation of “necessarily” or “possibly” inside the algebra of observables. The projection lattice of a Hilbert space gives an orthomodular quantum logic, not the classical modal logic S5, and the necessity operator of the ontological proof cannot be identified with, e.g., spectral projections or unitary evolution without adding an extraneous modal structure.

Kripke semantics for S5 is a metamathematical device for modal logic, not part of the physicist’s customary Hilbert-space apparatus. Within the customary setting one can formulate the first-order part of Gödel’s axioms about positive properties, but the modal axioms that drive the proof from “God-like is possibly existent” to “God-like is existent” are simply not expressible, let alone provable, in the usual QM mathematics. Hence existence of Gödel’s god-like entities cannot be established inside the customary mathematical formalism of quantum mechanics without first extending that formalism beyond what is standardly used.

2.text:
In the language in which Hilbert spaces, self-adjoint operators and the
spectral theorem are written down the physicist is using ordinary
classical mathematics, i.e. ZFC + analysis in the usual classical
first order logic.  In that metalanguage Gödel's ontological argument can
be written down as a perfectly normal derivation in classical first order
modal logic, normally S5, from the Gödel axioms for positivity

* P(x) is positive,
* if P(x) is positive and P(x)  →  Q(x) is provable then Q(x) is positive,
* if P(x) is positive then $\lnot P(x)$ is not positive,
* necessarily $\forall x\,[\,P(x)\rightarrow \Box P(x)\,]$,

and the crucial

* necessary existence is positive.

On that formal base the usual 26 line derivation

1.  $\exists x\,\forall P\,[P(x)\leftrightarrow P$ is positive$] \rightarrow \exists x\,\Box\forall P\,[P(x)\leftrightarrow P$ is positive$]$
 etc.

is a theorem of S5.  In particular the statement

$\exists x\,\forall P\,[P(x)\leftrightarrow P$ is positive$]$

i.e. there is a being which has exactly the positive properties, and in
particular possesses necessary existence, is a formal consequence of the
five positivity axioms.  That is why the argument is often said to be
formally valid.

It is valid and it can be coded in the very set theory and analysis in
which the complex Hilbert space $\mathcal H$, the algebra $B(\mathcal H)$
and the usual quantum mechanical formalism are defined.  What is not
obtained is a physical proof.  The positivity axioms, and in particular
the axiom that necessary existence is positive, are not theorems of
ZFC, nor are they theorems of quantum mechanics.  They are
metaphysical premises about the notion of a `positive property'.  The
derivation therefore gives at best a conditional mathematical theorem:

*If* you accept the Gödel axiomatisation of positivity in classical
logic, *then* the existence of a God-like, i.e. necessarily existent,
maximally positive, being is a formal consequence.

It is not a consequence of the Schrödinger equation, of the spectral
calculus, or of any proposition of the quantum mechanical formalism,
and it says nothing about existence in the physical world.  In the
scientific sense, and a fortiori in the quantum-logical reading in
which the propositional structure of quantum mechanics is an
orthomodular lattice and not a Boolean algebra, the classical modal
logic S5 that Gödel needs is not part of the physics.  Hence the
argument remains a conditional piece of formal philosophy, not a
theorem of quantum mechanics.

6.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: No. The mathematics that is taken as customary for quantum mechanics is the theory of separable complex Hilbert spaces and the corresponding †-algebras of bounded operators, with the usual first-order logic of set theory and complex analysis. That is a classical first-order setting with the standard interpretation of predicates as subsets of a Hilbert space or of the projection lattice. 

Gödel’s ontological argument for god-like entities, in the usual formulation, is essentially modal: it is a first-order modal theory in S5 with the necessity operator □ and the positivity axiom for properties. The proof requires an interpretation of □ and of the S5 accessibility relation, and the usual justification for it is Kripke semantics for modal logic.

Kripke semantics, the possible-worlds structure and the S5 modal operator, is not part of the customary Hilbert-space formalism of quantum mechanics. The formalism provides a representation of physical properties as projection operators and states as vectors or density operators, and the logic that is usually spoken of in that context is either classical predicate logic applied to the C*-algebra, or the orthomodular quantum logic of the projection lattice. Neither comes equipped with a canonical, internally definable modal operator whose Kripke interpretation lives inside the Hilbert space structure.

Embedding an S5 modal logic into a Hilbert space would require a substantial non-standard enrichment – e.g. adding a family of worlds, an accessibility relation and an interpretation of □ – which goes beyond the customary mathematics actually used to formulate and compute in quantum mechanics. Inside the unextended, customary setting there is therefore no canonical way to make sense of the modal axioms on which Gödel’s ontological proof rests, and the existence claim cannot be derived from the formalism as it is standardly employed.

The projection lattice gives orthomodular quantum logic, but it is interpreted in a classical meta-theory.

Gödel’s ontological argument is a first-order modal argument in S5 with positivity axioms:

Consensus from round 0:
* The argument is syntactically formalizable in the ZFC meta-theory in which Hilbert spaces live, and is valid in S5 conditional on the Gödel positivity axioms.
* The positivity axioms and the claim ◇∃x G(x) are metaphysical premises, not theorems of ZFC, arithmetic, or quantum mechanics. They are not about vectors, operators, spectra or Born probabilities.

* Hence there is no unconditional mathematical theorem about Hilbert spaces or numbers, and no physical proof from Schrödinger equation/spectral calculus. At best we get a conditional result: if you accept Gödel’s metaphysical positivity axioms in classical logic, then ∃x G(x) is a theorem of the background set theory/M-meta-theory.
* No new logical strength is added by QM; the argument remains formal philosophy, not a theorem of quantum mechanics.

Remaining nuance to track: distinction between “can be coded in the meta-theory that underlies QM” vs “is a theorem internal to the customary QM formalism”. Colleagues 1,2,5 stress conditional formalizability; colleagues 4,6,7 stress modal operator is not expressible without extending the formalism. Both point to no substantive proof. Unresolved is whether independence from ZFC is claimed; colleague 3 says existence is independent of ZFC, which may need clarification. Overall current belief: No unconditional proof in customary QM mathematics; only conditional formal derivability in the classical meta-theory.

The customary mathematics used for quantum mechanics is classical: ZFC set theory + analysis + first-order classical logic realised as separable complex Hilbert spaces H, self-adjoint operators, spectral measures, states as normalised positive linear functionals, etc. The projection lattice gives an orthomodular quantum logic but it is always interpreted in a classical meta-theory. No primitive modal operator □, no Kripke frame, no notion of “positive property’’ in Gödel’s sense is part of the Hilbert-space, C*-algebra or spectral calculus formalism.

Gödel’s ontological argument is a quantified modal argument in S5. With
P positive, P essentially positive = □P in all worlds where E exists,
G God-like = essentially has all positive properties,
and axioms A1 □P→P, A2 P→□P, closure of positivity and necessary existence is positive, plus ◇∃x G, S5 yields ∃x G and □∃x G. The derivation is formally valid in S5 and can be coded in the background set theory in which Hilbert spaces live.

That gives only a conditional meta-theoretic result: if you accept the Gödel positivity axioms and an S5 metaphysical necessity operator, then existence follows in the classical meta-theory that underlies QM. The positivity axioms, in particular that necessary existence is positive and P→□P, are not theorems of ZFC, arithmetic, functional analysis, the Schrödinger equation or C*-algebra theory. They are unformalised metaphysical premises.

Hence there is no proof of ∃x G(x) from the equations or formalism of quantum mechanics, and no canonical way to make □ or “essence of all positive properties’’ a vector/operator inside the customary Hilbert-space language. 2.text:
In the physics literature customary quantum mechanics is done in ordinary classical mathematics. 
States are vectors in a separable complex Hilbert space H, observables are self-adjoint operators on H, probabilities come from the spectral measure of a projection lattice.  All of that is defined in ZFC with classical first order logic, with analysis on top of it.  Quantum logic is just the orthomodular lattice P(H) interpreted in that classical meta-theory.

Gödel’s ontological argument is a derivation in quantified modal logic S5. With

* Pos(P): P is positive,
* Ess(x,P): P is essentially true of x,
* G(x):= ∀P[Pos(P) → Ess(x,P)],

and the usual Gödel axioms

A1 □P → P, A2 P → □P, A3 closure of Pos under implication and conjunction,
and in particular Necessary existence is positive,
and ◇∃x G(x),

S5 gives □◇∃x G(x) → ∃x G(x) and hence ∃x G(x) and □∃x G(x).

That derivation is perfectly formalizable in the set-theoretic meta-theory in which H, B(H), the spectral theorem etc. are defined. ZFC+classical logic is more than strong enough to code first-order modal logic and the finite list of positivity axioms. In that purely syntactic sense the ontological argument is a conditional theorem of the background set theory which underlies the Hilbert-space formalism: if the Gödel positivity axioms and S5 are accepted, the conclusion is a theorem of the meta-theory.

What is not obtained is a theorem of quantum mechanics. The positivity axioms, the notion of metaphysical necessity □, the S5 accessibility relation and the notion of an essence of all positive properties have no definition in the language of vectors, operators, spectra, states and expectation values. The customary QM formalism contains no primitive modal operator, no Kripke frame, and the projection lattice gives an orthomodular quantum logic, not S5. Identifying □ with spectral projections or unitary evolution is an extra enrichment, not part of the standard apparatus.

Hence unconditionally, from the Schrödinger equation, the spectral calculus or any physical postulate of quantum mechanics, the existence of a Gödelian god-like necessarily existent being is not derivable and cannot even be stated internally. At best one obtains the conditional, purely logical consistency statement:

If the Gödel metaphysical axioms for positivity and necessary existence are accepted in S5, then in the classical meta-theory in which quantum mechanics is written down there is a formal model with a God-like necessarily existent entity.

That is a conditional piece of formal philosophy, not a physical or mathematical theorem about Hilbert spaces and not a proof of the existence of Gödel’s god-like entities from the customary mathematics actually used for quantum mechanics.
